property_summary: For every input, C's owner() always returns the deployer (setUp's caller) and never the zero address, but the mutant returning address(0) makes owner() return address(0), breaking the rule.
For any admissible non-zero address, after the owner calls transferOwnership(a), owner() must return exactly a (and never the zero address); the mutant always returns address(0), breaking it.

For any nonzero address a, the contract owner can always successfully invoke the onlyOwner function setCaller(a) — because owner() returns the deployer and _checkOwner passes — but in the mutant owner() returns address(0), so every onlyOwner call, including setCaller(a), reverts for all callers.

For any admissible addresses, ownership transfer to a nonzero new owner always makes owner() return exactly that new owner, and the setCaller call from an arbitrary caller b succeeds exactly when b equals the address returned by owner(); the mutant returns address(0) from owner(), so for b = address(0) the two observations contradict each other.

For any nonzero address x, transferring ownership to x and then having x renounce succeeds and leaves owner() equal to address(0); the mutant's owner() always returns address(0), so every onlyOwner call (transferOwnership) reverts and the sequence fails for all x.

For any caller address, c.owner() must return the same immutable ownership address (independent of who queries it); the mutant returns the caller's own address, so for any caller other than the owner the two differ.

For any non-owner caller, calling transferOwnership must revert (only the stored owner can transfer ownership); the mutant makes owner() return the caller, so _checkOwner always passes and any non-owner can successfully transfer ownership.
For any caller, once the deployer has renounced ownership, c.owner() must return address(0); the mutant instead returns the caller's own (nonzero) address, breaking the rule.

Once ownership has been transferred to a new owner, any other address must no longer be able to call transferOwnership; the mutant makes owner() return the caller, so the previous owner (or anyone) can still transfer ownership.

owner() must return the same stored owner regardless of who queries it, so two distinct callers in the same state must observe identical owner() values; the mutant returns the caller's own address, so distinct callers observe different values.

For any caller, C.owner() must return the contract's stored owner (the deployer set at construction), but the mutant returns the contract's own address, which differs for any caller other than the token contract itself.
For any caller, the token's owner() must always return the actual owner address (the deployer), never the token contract's own address; the mutant makes owner() return address(c) for every input.
For every caller, c.owner() must return the immutable deployer set at construction (the test contract here), but the mutant always returns the token contract's own address instead.

For every caller, the token's owner() returns the deployer recorded at construction, which is never the token contract itself, so c.owner() must never equal address(c); the mutant returns address(this) from owner() for all callers, violating this invariant.

For any nonzero fuzzed address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the deployer (the stored owner returned by owner()) must succeed and make owner() equal that address; the mutant's owner() returns address(c) instead of the stored owner, so the onlyOwner check reverts for every caller including the deployer.
